screens.title: Special Methods (Dunder Methods) Revisited
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter you'll move from knowing simple dunder methods to confidently designing classes that integrate with Python's language features. We'll focus on developer-facing representations with repr and user-facing strings with str, correct equality with eq, and the crucial link between equality and hashing. You'll also learn how to implement sequence and mapping protocols so your objects support len, indexing, slicing, assignment, and deletion. These skills make your types behave like native Python types, improving readability, debugging, and library interoperability. For example, a well-formed repr helps debugging tools and logging, while a correct hash avoids subtle bugs when using instances as dict keys or set members. We'll also highlight common mistakes: returning inconsistent hashes after overriding equality, failing to support slices, and forgetting NotImplemented in cross-type comparisons. Throughout, you'll see concrete code examples for a Vector, a MyCustomList, and a Polynomial starter implementation. By the end you should know when to make objects hashable, how to implement index handling, and how to present clear developer and user representations. Consider this chapter a set of practical recipes that help your custom types act like first-class citizens. Ready to explore these dunder patterns and their real consequences?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the skills you'll build with Python's special methods. First, you'll understand why dunder methods are part of the object model and learn common use cases beyond initialization and simple string conversions. Practically, this means recognizing when to implement methods so your objects integrate with functions like len, repr, and slice operations. Second, you'll be able to implement repr and eq correctly for clear developer tooling and reliable comparisons — including returning NotImplemented when cross-type comparisons are not supported. Third, you'll grasp the required relationship between eq and hash so you can decide when an object should be hashable, implement a safe hash from immutable attributes, or explicitly set hash to None for mutable objects. Fourth, you'll implement sequence and mapping protocols using len, getitem, setitem, and delitem, handling integer indices and slice objects properly. Each objective includes hands-on examples and common pitfalls to train both correctness and idiomatic style. By the end, you'll have code patterns and checks to avoid subtle bugs in collections and debugging workflows. These skills matter because well-behaved objects are easier to test, maintain, and compose with Python libraries.

screens.title: __repr__ vs __str__
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the difference between repr and str clearly. repr is intended to be an unambiguous representation suitable for developers and debugging; its ideal output often looks like a constructor call that could recreate the object. By contrast, str produces a readable summary for end users and is what the print function uses. A concrete example: a Vector object might have repr that returns "Vector(1, 2, 3)" while str returns "(1, 2, 3)". That separation matters because debug logs and interactive consoles rely on repr to show precise state, while output exposed to users should be concise and friendly. A common misconception is that repr must always be valid Python code; while that is a useful guideline, the practical goal is unambiguity and debugging convenience. Another pitfall is implementing only str and expecting debugging tools to show the same informative text; when repr is missing, repr will fall back to the default, less helpful object description. Example check: if you implement repr but not str, the print function will use repr as a fallback. Takeaway: implement both when possible—design repr to aid developers and str for readable displays. Question to reflect on: what parts of an object’s state are essential to include in repr to make debugging reliable?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › __repr__ vs __str__
Definition & Purpose
Understand the intended audiences and goals for each method.
  • __repr__: unambiguous, developer-focused; ideal output resembles constructor call.
  • __str__: readable, user-focused; used by the print function and str().
  • Fallback rules: if __str__ missing, repr is used; if __repr__ missing, default object repr appears.
Example
Vector(1, 2, 3) vs (1, 2, 3)
Misconception
Assuming __repr__ must always be valid code; prioritize clarity and reproducibility where practical.
Key Takeaway

Provide an unambiguous repr for debugging and a concise str for user-facing output.

Code Example (Vector)
class Vector: def __init__(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def __repr__(self): return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y}, {self.z})" def __str__(self): return f"({self.x}, {self.y}, {self.z})" # print(v) uses __str__, repr(v) uses __repr__
Try: implement both and inspect outputs with the print function and the interactive prompt to see how tools present your object.

screens.title: Implementing __repr__ for Debuggability
screens.narratorSegment: In this walkthrough we'll implement a clear repr for a simple Vector class and discuss choices about what to include. The goal of repr is to show enough state so a developer can diagnose issues; a common practice is to format the string like a constructor: Vector(1, 2, 3). Include the minimal attributes that define the object's identity. Concrete example: if x, y, and z are the core properties for equality and hash, include them. A typical mistake is including transient or large internal caches in repr, which clutters debugging. Another pitfall is exposing secrets or huge binary blobs; keep repr concise. When you can't safely reproduce the object via the string, still aim for a stable, clear format that shows the relevant attributes and types. After implementing repr, run repr(instance) and inspect logs and REPL outputs. Ask yourself whether someone reading logs could reconstruct the important state. Takeaway: prefer clarity and reproducibility for repr, avoid leaking sensitive or noisy internals, and use the constructor-like format when practical. Now, implement and run the Vector example, checking how tools use repr in tracebacks and interactive shells.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Implementing __repr__
Walkthrough: Vector.__repr__
Aim for a constructor-style, unambiguous format including only the attributes that define identity.
class Vector:
  def __init__(self, x, y, z):
    self.x = x
    self.y = y
    self.z = z

  def __repr__(self):
    return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y}, {self.z})"

# Usage
v = Vector(1, 2, 3)
print(repr(v))  # Vector(1, 2, 3)
Common mistake: including mutable caches or private large fields in repr. Instead, show the small set of attributes that are stable and relevant for debugging.
Quick Checks
  • Is the output concise and unambiguous?
  • Could a developer understand the object's identity from the repr?
  • Does the repr avoid exposing secrets or huge data?
Key Takeaway

Make repr reproducible and focused on the attributes that matter for debugging.

screens.title: __eq__ semantics and NotImplemented
screens.narratorSegment: Equality is a contract: when two objects compare equal using the equality operator, that result should reflect your class's notion of identity. Implement eq to compare the attributes that define equivalence. A clear pattern is to return NotImplemented if the other operand is not of a compatible type; that allows Python to try the reverse comparison or fall back gracefully. For example, Vector. eq should check isinstance(other, Vector) and then compare x, y, and z. A common mistake is returning False when types differ, which prevents the other object's eq from being tried and can break symmetric behavior when subclasses are involved. Another pitfall is performing comparisons that raise exceptions for unexpected other types; instead, return NotImplemented so Python can handle it. Concrete example: if you compare a Vector with a tuple, many designs prefer to return NotImplemented so tuple's comparison logic can run or the result defaults to False consistently. Closing takeaway: implement type checks, compare identity-defining attributes, and return NotImplemented for unsupported types. Reflection: when might you intentionally allow comparisons to other container types, and how would you document that?

keyIdea.text: In __eq__, check type compatibility, compare identity attributes, and return NotImplemented for unsupported types.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › __eq__ semantics
What to do in __eq__

Check type compatibility, compare the attributes that determine equality, and return NotImplemented for unsupported operand types.

def __eq__(self, other): if not isinstance(other, Vector): return NotImplemented return (self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y and self.z == other.z) # Behavior: if other is not a Vector, Python will attempt other.__eq__(self) or fall back to False
Concrete example
v1 == v2 True when components match; comparing with unrelated types should return NotImplemented to allow symmetric logic.
Misconception
Returning False for different types prevents the other operand's comparison path and can break symmetric equals with subclasses.

screens.title: __hash__ and the equality contract
screens.narratorSegment: Hashing and equality are tied by a simple rule: if two objects compare equal, their hash values must be equal. If you override eq without also providing a compatible hash, Python will make instances unhashable to avoid broken dicts and sets. That means attempting to place such an instance into a set or dict key will raise a TypeError. Use hash only when your objects are immutable or their identity attributes are immutable. A safe pattern is to compute the hash from a tuple of the attributes that determine equality, for example hash((self. x, self. y, self. z)). If your object's state can change after creation, explicitly set hash = None to communicate unhashability. A common mistake is leaving a mutable object hashable because the hash value would change after mutation, making lookup impossible or incorrect in hash-based collections. Concrete example: two Vector instances with identical components should have the same hash so they behave correctly as set members. Takeaway: decide hashability based on immutability and always keep eq and hash consistent. Question: what design or documentation steps help users of your class understand whether it is safe to use instances as dict keys?

keyIdea.title: Hash rule
keyIdea.text: If objects compare equal, they must have equal hashes. Make mutable objects unhashable and compute hashes from immutable identity attributes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › __hash__ and equality
Why hash matters

Hash-based collections rely on stable hash values. If equality changes while an object is inside a set, collection integrity breaks.

# Safe hash for immutable Vector
def __hash__(self):
  return hash((self.x, self.y, self.z))

# For mutable classes:
# __hash__ = None  # marks instances unhashable
Common error: making a mutable object hashable. That leads to hard-to-find bugs when the object is used as a key and then mutated.
Concrete check
After implementing __eq__ and __hash__, verify that two equal instances have equal hashes and behave correctly in sets and dicts.
Common Mistake

Failing to set __hash__ = None for mutable objects causes inconsistent behavior in hash collections.

screens.title: Sequence and Mapping Protocols
screens.narratorSegment: Container protocols make your classes behave like lists, tuples, or dicts. Implementing len enables the len function; it must return a non-negative integer. getitem defines access via square brackets and must accept integers for index access and slice objects for slicing. For mapping-like behavior, getitem may accept hashable keys and should raise KeyError when a key is missing. setitem handles assignment, supporting integer indices and slices for sequences, and delitem removes items. A concrete example is a custom list wrapper that stores data internally and implements these dunders to expose list-like behavior. A common mistake is not supporting slice objects in getitem, which produces TypeError when users attempt slicing. Another error is returning the wrong exception type — sequences should use IndexError for out-of-range integer indices, while mappings should use KeyError. When designing these methods, think about the expected semantics: if you support negative indices and slicing semantics like built-ins, document that behavior. Takeaway: choose sequence or mapping semantics and implement the correct return and error types to match Python expectations. Sequence and Mapping Protocols means match built-in semantics: return integer from __len__, support slices in __getitem__, and raise indexerror or keyerror appropriately.. In practical terms, how __len__, __getitem__, __setitem__, and __delitem__ create natural containers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Sequence & Mapping Protocols
Protocol overview

Implement these methods to let users call len(), use indexing and slicing, and mutate your container with familiar syntax.

__len__
Return the non-negative integer count of items.
__getitem__
Accept int and slice for sequences; accept hashable keys for mappings. Raise IndexError or KeyError as appropriate.
__setitem__
Support assignments and slice assignments with consistent behavior.
__delitem__
Remove items by index or key; ensure correct exception types on invalid deletions.
Key Takeaway

Design your container semantics explicitly and follow built-in exception and slicing conventions for predictable behavior.

screens.title: MyCustomList: __len__ and __getitem__
screens.narratorSegment: We will implement the fundamental read operations for a custom sequence: len and getitem. len should return an integer equal to the number of accessible elements. For getitem, support both integers and slice objects. When receiving an integer index, enforce valid bounds and support negative indices with the usual Python semantics. When receiving a slice, return a new instance of your custom container holding the sliced data. A concrete implementation pattern is to wrap an internal list and delegate operations, returning a MyCustomList for slices. A frequent mistake is to forget negative index handling or to raise the wrong exception; sequences should raise IndexError for out-of-range integer indices. Another subtle issue is returning a raw list for slices instead of your custom type, breaking A P I consistency. Example: MyCustomList. getitem checks isinstance(key, int) and isinstance(key, slice) separately, returning an item or a new MyCustomList respectively; otherwise it raises TypeError. Takeaway: mirror built-in behaviors for indexing and slicing so users of your container encounter familiar semantics. Try running the sample code and slicing with [:2], [-1], and out-of-range indices to see error handling.

keyIdea.title: Index handling
keyIdea.text: Support int and slice keys; raise IndexError for bad integer indices and return your container type for slices.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › MyCustomList: len & getitem
Starter implementation
class MyCustomList:
  def __init__(self, initial_data=None):
    self._data = list(initial_data) if initial_data is not None else []

  def __len__(self):
    return len(self._data)

  def __getitem__(self, key):
    if isinstance(key, int):
      if not (-len(self._data) <= key < len(self._data)):
        raise IndexError("Index out of range")
      return self._data[key]
    elif isinstance(key, slice):
      return MyCustomList(self._data[key])
    else:
      raise TypeError("Key must be an integer or slice")
Run examples: access positive and negative indices, slice ranges, and check len to verify the returned counts match expectations.
Checks & Examples
Try:
my_list = MyCustomList([10,20,30,40]) len(my_list) # 4 my_list[2] # 30 my_list[-1] # 40 my_list[1:3] # MyCustomList([20,30])
Common Mistake

Returning a plain list for slices breaks the container interface. Return the same custom type for consistency.

screens.title: __setitem__ and __delitem__
screens.narratorSegment: Now we extend the custom list with assignment and deletion. setitem must accept integer indices and slices. For integers, validate bounds and then assign directly into the backing list. For slices, expect an iterable on the right-hand side and replace the slice accordingly. delitem should remove the item or slice similarly. A concrete example: if my_list[1:3] = [7,8], the internal list must update those indices. Common pitfalls include not validating the iterable type for slice assignment and accidentally creating inconsistent length or type errors. Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › __setitem__ & __delitem__
Mutating the container
  def __setitem__(self, key, value):
    if isinstance(key, int):
      if not (-len(self._data) <= key < len(self._data)):
        raise IndexError("Index out of range")
      self._data[key] = value
    elif isinstance(key, slice):
      self._data[key] = list(value)  # accept any iterable
    else:
      raise TypeError("Key must be an integer or slice")

  def __delitem__(self, key):
    if isinstance(key, int):
      del self._data[key]
    elif isinstance(key, slice):
      del self._data[key]
    else:
      raise TypeError("Key must be an integer or slice")
Test assignments with single indices, different-length slice replacements, and deletions to ensure the internal structure remains consistent.

screens.title: Common mistakes and defensive strategies
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson groups common mistakes and defensive techniques. First, inconsistent eq and hash implementations cause hard-to-find bugs in sets and dictionaries. Defensive step: when implementing eq, always review whether the object should be hashable; if not, set hash = None. Second, neglecting NotImplemented in eq prevents symmetric comparisons and can break subclass equality. Defensive step: return NotImplemented for incompatible types. Third, incorrect exception types in container methods — returning TypeError instead of IndexError or KeyError — confuses users and libraries. Defensive step: follow built-in semantics and write tests for edge cases. Fourth, exposing sensitive or very large internals in repr can leak data or clutter logs; keep repr concise and focused on identity. Lastly, failing to support slice objects produces surprising TypeError for slicing; test integer and slice cases separately. Concrete strategy: add unit tests that assert set/dict behavior for equal objects, test slicing and negative indices, and include invariants to ensure your object's hash is stable when expected. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you'll move from knowing simple dunder methods to confidently designing classes that integrate with Python's language features. We'll focus on developer-facing representations with repr and user-facing strings with str, correct equality with eq, and the crucial link between equality and hashing. You'll also learn how to implement sequence and mapping protocols so your objects support len, indexing, slicing, assignment, and deletion. These skills make your types behave like native Python types, improving readability, debugging, and library interoperability. For example, a well-formed repr helps debugging tools and logging, while a correct hash avoids subtle bugs when using instances as dict keys or set members. We'll also highlight common mistakes: returning inconsistent hashes after overriding equality, failing to support slices, and forgetting NotImplemented in cross-type comparisons. Throughout, you'll see concrete code examples for a Vector, a MyCustomList, and a Polynomial starter implementation. By the end you should know when to make objects hashable, how to implement index handling, and how to present clear developer and user representations. Consider this chapter a set of practical recipes that help your custom types act like first-class citizens. Ready to explore these dunder patterns and their real consequences?

These objectives guide the skills you'll build with Python's special methods. First, you'll understand why dunder methods are part of the object model and learn common use cases beyond initialization and simple string conversions. Practically, this means recognizing when to implement methods so your objects integrate with functions like len, repr, and slice operations. Second, you'll be able to implement repr and eq correctly for clear developer tooling and reliable comparisons — including returning NotImplemented when cross-type comparisons are not supported. Third, you'll grasp the required relationship between eq and hash so you can decide when an object should be hashable, implement a safe hash from immutable attributes, or explicitly set hash to None for mutable objects. Fourth, you'll implement sequence and mapping protocols using len, getitem, setitem, and delitem, handling integer indices and slice objects properly. Each objective includes hands-on examples and common pitfalls to train both correctness and idiomatic style. By the end, you'll have code patterns and checks to avoid subtle bugs in collections and debugging workflows. These skills matter because well-behaved objects are easier to test, maintain, and compose with Python libraries.

This second objectives slide sets the practice focus. You'll implement examples that prove your knowledge: a Vector that exposes both a developer-friendly representation and a human-friendly string; equality semantics that respect type checks and return NotImplemented when appropriate; and a MyCustomList that supports slices, indexing, assignment, and deletion without surprising errors. You will also practice the decision tree for hashing: if your class is immutable and equality depends on its immutable attributes, implement hash that combines those attributes; if it's mutable, set hash to None and document why. Practically, we will exercise these with code you can run: live-coding the Vector and MyCustomList, and a Polynomial starter for the hands-on activity. The exercises reinforce correct exception types — IndexError for out-of-range sequence access and KeyError for missing mapping keys — and stress consistent A P I design so your classes behave predictably. Expect to spend time reading console outputs to verify repr, equality, hashing, and container operations so you can recognize and fix the most common mistakes quickly.

Let's define the difference between repr and str clearly. repr is intended to be an unambiguous representation suitable for developers and debugging; its ideal output often looks like a constructor call that could recreate the object. By contrast, str produces a readable summary for end users and is what the print function uses. A concrete example: a Vector object might have repr that returns "Vector(1, 2, 3)" while str returns "(1, 2, 3)". That separation matters because debug logs and interactive consoles rely on repr to show precise state, while output exposed to users should be concise and friendly. A common misconception is that repr must always be valid Python code; while that is a useful guideline, the practical goal is unambiguity and debugging convenience. Another pitfall is implementing only str and expecting debugging tools to show the same informative text; when repr is missing, repr will fall back to the default, less helpful object description. Example check: if you implement repr but not str, the print function will use repr as a fallback. Takeaway: implement both when possible—design repr to aid developers and str for readable displays. Question to reflect on: what parts of an object’s state are essential to include in repr to make debugging reliable?

In this walkthrough we'll implement a clear repr for a simple Vector class and discuss choices about what to include. The goal of repr is to show enough state so a developer can diagnose issues; a common practice is to format the string like a constructor: Vector(1, 2, 3). Include the minimal attributes that define the object's identity. Concrete example: if x, y, and z are the core properties for equality and hash, include them. A typical mistake is including transient or large internal caches in repr, which clutters debugging. Another pitfall is exposing secrets or huge binary blobs; keep repr concise. When you can't safely reproduce the object via the string, still aim for a stable, clear format that shows the relevant attributes and types. After implementing repr, run repr(instance) and inspect logs and REPL outputs. Ask yourself whether someone reading logs could reconstruct the important state. Takeaway: prefer clarity and reproducibility for repr, avoid leaking sensitive or noisy internals, and use the constructor-like format when practical. Now, implement and run the Vector example, checking how tools use repr in tracebacks and interactive shells.

Equality is a contract: when two objects compare equal using the equality operator, that result should reflect your class's notion of identity. Implement eq to compare the attributes that define equivalence. A clear pattern is to return NotImplemented if the other operand is not of a compatible type; that allows Python to try the reverse comparison or fall back gracefully. For example, Vector. eq should check isinstance(other, Vector) and then compare x, y, and z. A common mistake is returning False when types differ, which prevents the other object's eq from being tried and can break symmetric behavior when subclasses are involved. Another pitfall is performing comparisons that raise exceptions for unexpected other types; instead, return NotImplemented so Python can handle it. Concrete example: if you compare a Vector with a tuple, many designs prefer to return NotImplemented so tuple's comparison logic can run or the result defaults to False consistently. Closing takeaway: implement type checks, compare identity-defining attributes, and return NotImplemented for unsupported types. Reflection: when might you intentionally allow comparisons to other container types, and how would you document that?

Hashing and equality are tied by a simple rule: if two objects compare equal, their hash values must be equal. If you override eq without also providing a compatible hash, Python will make instances unhashable to avoid broken dicts and sets. That means attempting to place such an instance into a set or dict key will raise a TypeError. Use hash only when your objects are immutable or their identity attributes are immutable. A safe pattern is to compute the hash from a tuple of the attributes that determine equality, for example hash((self. x, self. y, self. z)). If your object's state can change after creation, explicitly set hash = None to communicate unhashability. A common mistake is leaving a mutable object hashable because the hash value would change after mutation, making lookup impossible or incorrect in hash-based collections. Concrete example: two Vector instances with identical components should have the same hash so they behave correctly as set members. Takeaway: decide hashability based on immutability and always keep eq and hash consistent. Question: what design or documentation steps help users of your class understand whether it is safe to use instances as dict keys?

Container protocols make your classes behave like lists, tuples, or dicts. Implementing len enables the len function; it must return a non-negative integer. getitem defines access via square brackets and must accept integers for index access and slice objects for slicing. For mapping-like behavior, getitem may accept hashable keys and should raise KeyError when a key is missing. setitem handles assignment, supporting integer indices and slices for sequences, and delitem removes items. A concrete example is a custom list wrapper that stores data internally and implements these dunders to expose list-like behavior. A common mistake is not supporting slice objects in getitem, which produces TypeError when users attempt slicing. Another error is returning the wrong exception type — sequences should use IndexError for out-of-range integer indices, while mappings should use KeyError. When designing these methods, think about the expected semantics: if you support negative indices and slicing semantics like built-ins, document that behavior. Takeaway: choose sequence or mapping semantics and implement the correct return and error types to match Python expectations. For getitem, support both integers and slice objects. When receiving an integer index, enforce valid bounds and support negative indices with the usual Python semantics. Defensive step: when implementing eq, always review whether the object should be hashable; if not, set hash = None. Second, neglecting NotImplemented in eq prevents symmetric comparisons and can break subclass equality. Defensive step: return NotImplemented for incompatible types. Third, incorrect exception types in container methods — returning TypeError instead of IndexError or KeyError — confuses users and libraries. Defensive step: follow built-in semantics and write tests for edge cases. Fourth, exposing sensitive or very large internals in repr can leak data or clutter logs; keep repr concise and focused on identity. Lastly, failing to support slice objects produces surprising TypeError for slicing; test integer and slice cases separately. Concrete strategy: add unit tests that assert set/dict behavior for equal objects, test slicing and negative indices, and include invariants to ensure your object's hash is stable when expected. Let's summarize the core ideas. First, special methods let your custom classes participate naturally in Python: representational methods like repr and str serve different audiences and both are valuable. Second, equality and hashing form a contract: override eq thoughtfully, return NotImplemented for incompatible types, and ensure equal objects produce equal hashes or set hash to None for mutable objects. Third, sequence and mapping protocols let your objects behave like built-ins; implement len, getitem, setitem, and delitem with correct behavior for integers and slices and appropriate exception types. These practices make your classes debuggable, composable, and safe to use in collections. A quick mental checklist: does your repr capture identity? Does eq compare the correct attributes? Is your object immutable if it is hashable? Does your container support slices and raise correct exceptions? Use unit tests to verify these properties. Good implementations reduce surprising runtime errors and make your code easier to maintain and reuse.

Rule two: if you override equality, decide if your instances are safely hashable; if they are immutable, compute the hash from the identity attributes, otherwise set hash to None. Rule three: when exposing container behavior, mirror built-in semantics for indexing, slicing, and exceptions so users experience the familiar Python behavior.
